title: Special Cases
summary: Internal transfers, relocation, visa sponsorship, and new-grad hiring each diverge from the standard external-hire playbook — different levers are available, and applying standard tactics to the wrong case can backfire.

slides.markdown:
Everything covered so far in this group assumes a standard external hire negotiating a single offer with a company that has no prior claim on the relationship. Four common situations diverge from that in ways that change what's actually negotiable: internal transfers or promotions, relocation packages, visa-sponsored hires, and new-grad offers.

Each case has its own constraints — some tighter than a standard external negotiation, some looser in specific unexpected ways. Applying the standard playbook unmodified to any of these is a common mistake, because the same tactic that works for an external hire (competing offer, deadline extension, aggressive counter) can be structurally unavailable, or even risky, in these cases.

slides.sectionTitle: Internal transfer or promotion: what's negotiable vs. fixed by policy
slides.markdown:
Internal moves are governed by HR policy far more rigidly than external offers — most companies apply a **standard raise percentage band** for a given promotion or transfer (commonly a fixed range like 8-15% for a level-up), and a hiring manager or HR partner often can't exceed that band without an unusual exception, regardless of how much they personally want to pay you more.

What's usually still negotiable: the **new role's scope and title** (sometimes more flexible than the comp band itself), the timing of the transfer relative to your next review cycle, and whether unvested equity from your current role transfers cleanly or needs a fresh grant negotiated separately.

What's rarely negotiable: the percentage increase itself, since internal equity concerns (a transfer getting a bigger raise than a peer's annual review) make HR very protective of that specific number — pushing hard there is more likely to stall the move than to move the number.

slides.sectionTitle: Relocation packages: what's typically covered and what to ask for
slides.markdown:
Standard relocation packages usually cover: shipping of household goods, a set number of nights of temporary housing (commonly 2-4 weeks), and often a flat lump sum for miscellaneous costs (typically $2-10k depending on distance and level). What's frequently **not** included by default, but is reasonable to ask for: a house-hunting trip before the move, temporary housing extended beyond the standard window if your lease timing doesn't align, or a **tax gross-up** on the relocation payment itself (relocation reimbursements are often taxable income, so a $10k package can net meaningfully less after tax unless grossed up).

A specific, practical ask: "is the relocation package tax-assisted, or will I need to account for the tax burden myself?" is a normal, expected question that surfaces a real cost most candidates don't think to ask about until their first paycheck.

slides.sectionTitle: Visa sponsorship constraints on leverage and timelines
slides.markdown:
A candidate needing visa sponsorship (commonly H-1B in the US, or equivalent skilled-worker visas elsewhere) faces two structural constraints a citizen or existing-work-authorization candidate doesn't. First, **fewer companies sponsor at all** — some smaller companies or those without established immigration programs simply won't, which narrows which offers exist as leverage in the first place. Second, **switching jobs has real transfer risk and timeline cost** — a visa transfer between employers can take weeks to months depending on the visa type and country, and an aggressive negotiation stance risking the offer is a much higher-stakes bet when the alternative isn't just "look elsewhere" but potentially a real gap in work authorization.

This doesn't mean no leverage exists — a genuine competing offer from another sponsoring company is still real leverage — but bluffing, aggressive deadlines, or walking away as a tactic carry meaningfully higher personal risk here than for a candidate without sponsorship constraints, and should be weighed accordingly.

slides.sectionTitle: New-grad offers: less room, different levers
slides.markdown:
New-grad compensation is usually the most standardized band in a company's entire ladder — many companies pay every new grad at a given level almost identically, specifically to avoid the appearance of unfairness among a large cohort hired together. This means base salary negotiation room is often genuinely minimal, sometimes effectively zero, regardless of how well a candidate argues.

The levers that remain: **sign-on bonus** (often has more per-candidate flexibility than base, since it doesn't set an ongoing comp precedent visible to the whole cohort), **start date** (can matter for finishing a degree, an internship payout, or personal timing), and, less commonly, **level itself** if a candidate has unusually strong pre-grad experience (significant internships, notable open-source work, research). Directly asking for a base bump that a peer wouldn't also get is the most likely ask to be flatly declined in this specific case.

slides.sectionTitle: External-hire leverage tactics vs. what's actually available internally
slides.subTitle: Compare
slides.markdown:
| Tactic | External hire | Internal transfer/promotion |
|---|---|---|
| Competing offer | Strong, standard leverage | Rarely usable directly — an external offer can still prompt a counter-retention conversation, but it's a different, riskier conversation than a same-company transfer negotiation |
| Anchoring a target number | Normal and expected | Often moot — comp increase is frequently capped by a fixed policy band regardless of anchor |
| Deadline pressure | A real, common lever (exploding offers) | Rarely applies — internal moves usually run on much longer, calendar-driven timelines (review cycles) |
| What actually moves the outcome | Comp number itself | Scope, title, and timing of the move relative to the next review cycle |

The biggest mistake in this comparison is treating an internal move like an external negotiation and pushing hard on a comp number that's structurally fixed, while missing the scope and timing levers that are actually flexible.

slides.sectionTitle: Applying standard leverage tactics to a visa-constrained offer
slides.subTitle: Pitfall
slides.markdown:
A candidate reading generic negotiation advice ("be willing to walk," "issue a firm deadline") and applying it unmodified to a visa-sponsored situation risks a much worse outcome than the same tactic would produce for an unconstrained candidate. Walking from a sponsoring offer isn't a symmetric risk when the realistic alternative set of sponsoring employers is smaller, and a delayed start over a stalled negotiation can interact badly with visa timing (status gaps, grace periods) in ways that have nothing to do with the comp conversation itself.

The safer approach: still negotiate, using genuine evidence (market data, real competing offers from other sponsoring companies) — but weight the relationship and certainty of the offer more heavily than a candidate without sponsorship constraints would, and avoid any tactic (bluffing, hard ultimatums) that risks the one sponsoring offer in hand for a marginal comp gain.

slides.sectionTitle: Internal promotion timing: before or after the cycle
slides.markdown:
A specific, high-leverage question for internal moves: does the raise take effect at the transfer date, or does it wait for the next formal review cycle (often 6-9 months later)? Some companies default to the latter unless a candidate specifically asks, which can mean doing the new, higher-scoped job at the old comp level for most of a year.

Asking directly — "will the comp adjustment take effect at the transfer date, or do I need to wait for the next cycle" — surfaces this before it becomes a surprise, and in many companies it's a genuinely negotiable timing question even when the raise percentage itself isn't. This is a clean example of the broader pattern in this topic: the number is fixed, but a specific adjacent term (timing, scope, title) usually isn't, and asking about it costs nothing.

slides.sectionTitle: A worked example: negotiating a relocation gap
slides.subTitle: Concrete example
slides.markdown:
```
Situation: Offer includes a $8k relocation lump sum, no mention of tax
treatment. Candidate estimates actual moving costs (movers, temporary
housing gap, flights) at roughly $11k, and knows lump-sum relocation
payments are typically taxed as ordinary income.

Candidate's ask:
"Thanks for including relocation support. Two quick questions: is the
$8k lump sum tax-assisted, and is there flexibility to increase it given
my estimated actual costs are closer to $11k for a cross-country move?"

Typical outcome: recruiter confirms the $8k is NOT grossed up (meaning
after ~30% effective tax, the candidate nets roughly $5.6k), and offers
either a modest increase to the lump sum or a tax gross-up on the
existing amount, whichever is easier for their policy to approve.
```

The key move is asking a specific, informed question rather than a vague "can you help more with relocation" — naming the tax mechanic by name signals the candidate has actually done the math, which tends to get a more substantive response.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading which case you're actually in
slides.markdown:
The senior-level skill across all four special cases is the same: before applying any tactic from earlier in this group, correctly identify which constraints actually govern this specific negotiation. An internal transfer candidate who tries to anchor a number like an external hire wastes effort on a lever that's policy-capped. A visa-sponsored candidate who bluffs a competing offer risks more than a citizen candidate making the identical bluff. A new grad pushing hard on base salary is fighting the one lever with the least flexibility in the entire package.

In each case, the standard tactics from [negotiation tactics and scripts](negotiation-tactics-scripts) and [competing offers and leverage](competing-offers-leverage) still apply in spirit — evidence-based asks, collaborative tone, knowing which lever actually moves — but the specific lever that's flexible shifts, and correctly identifying that shift before negotiating is most of the work.

These four cases aren't exhaustive — contractor-to-full-time conversions, acquihires, and boomerang rehires all have their own quirks — but they share the same underlying lesson: comp negotiation isn't one universal script. [Understanding levels and comp bands](levels-comp-bands) and [reading and evaluating an offer](reading-evaluating-offer) give you the foundation to evaluate any offer; this topic is the reminder to check, case by case, which of those foundations actually apply before you negotiate.
